title: This Designer's Secret: "The More Ordinary, the More Wondrous" | A Curious Person
excerpt: Oki Sato and his studio Nendo show why design is a part of business that business cannot do without.
body:
Oki Sato and his studio Nendo show why design is a part of business that business cannot do without.

## Who he is: Oki Sato (born 1977), a Japanese designer who founded the design studio Nendo in Tokyo in 2002. Working across furniture, interiors, products, clothing and accessories, Sato and his team usually juggle more than 250 projects at once and turn out around 50 finished works a year. Newsweek once named him one of "the 100 Japanese most respected by the world."

## His curiosity: "Giving people a small '!' moment."

Had it not been for the 2002 Milan furniture fair, Oki Sato might have stayed on the path to becoming an architect.

Born in Toronto, Sato moved back to Japan at ten. He studied architecture at Waseda University and stayed on for graduate work in the same field. But a graduation trip to Milan made him change careers before his first one had even begun.

That April in Milan, the scale of the international design event hit him hard. "For the first time we realized how many architects were also designing furniture and products, and how design made every corner of life better. It felt like we were seeing the future of design."

Determined that his own work would one day be shown there, Sato went home and founded Nendo. Within three years he had opened a branch in Milan, the capital of modern design. He also fulfilled the wish he made on that first trip: at Milan Design Week 2015, Nendo staged a retrospective of more than 100 products it had created over the previous year for 19 brands.

![Nendo Works 2014-2015 at Milan Design Week](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150536viHIce7DX4bMwAKu.jpg-w600)

![Nendo Works 2014-2015 at Milan Design Week](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150536qYQIfKZx2E0gATas.jpg-w600)

Today Nendo is a regular at international design shows and award ceremonies. It has won Germany's Red Dot Design Award, Designer of the Year from both ***Wallpaper*** and ***ELLE DECO***, Designer of the Year at Maison & Objet Paris, and more Japanese design prizes than anyone can count. Sato himself made Newsweek's list of "the 100 Japanese most respected by the world," and his best-known works are in the collections of the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Victoria and Albert Museum, the Centre Pompidou and other major museums.

But Japan has a mature design industry and no shortage of strong designers. Is Sato an exception?

Every era in Japan has produced star industrial designers, from the older generation of Sori Yanagi and Kenji Ekuan to Naoto Fukasawa and Kenya Hara, who were much admired in China a few years ago. Nearly all of them hold firm views of what design should express. Yanagi called for "feeling with your hands how an object fits the person, stripping away clutter and ornament to make plain objects of the greatest practical beauty." Hara champions "Re-Design," and Fukasawa "Without Thought."

Each has his own strengths, but they share something: even as they absorbed Western influence, they stayed true to their own traditions. Their work is simple and clean. Many people see this as the Zen spirit of Japanese design, but in substance it is closer to a preference for function over playfulness.

Japan produces designers in abundance, and many carry on either the Zen spirit or the clean, functional style. Sato loosens our idea of Japanese design a little. Perhaps because he spent his childhood in Canada, his thinking is not "very Japanese." He does not chase Japanese rigor or Zen calm. He puts more weight on playfulness, with function wrapped inside it. And he treats design as a business, giving marketing equal or even greater weight.

"A good product will always find buyers" is not a rule Sato accepts. How can you sell something without showing people why it is worth having?

Take HALSUIT, the menswear chain Nendo designed for the Japanese company Haruyama Shoji in 2011. Sato moved the fitting rooms, normally tucked into a corner, to the middle of the shop, and set out DVD players and magazines for the people who come along to keep shoppers company. He also made the shop feel like the kind of office where you would wear a suit. Each HALSUIT entrance looks like a company reception desk, the cabinets hold rows of neatly hung shirts, and even the chairs are all the same model and color, as in a conference room.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150537i7t3Sb1Q6MCcHgm5.jpg-w600)

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150537TC05NFwdkOHeQfYG.jpg-w600)

![A HALSUIT suit store](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150538zQu9dhbWZt3Rsy0A.jpg-w600)

Masafumi Haruyama, president of Haruyama Shoji, still remembers what Sato told him at their first meeting: "Design has to get customers to buy the product, by whatever means the designer has. If it doesn't do that, however good the work is, it's wasted." After the HALSUIT Higashi-Okayama store opened in autumn 2011, suit sales rose 10% over the previous year, prices rose 40%, and customers stayed in the store 40% longer.

Sato has never thought of himself as an artist. He doesn't fuss over small differences in detail, and he knows clients don't want flights of fancy. If he were designing a tree, he would start not with the leaves but with the trunk and roots. Applied to brands, that means getting the "trunk" and "roots" right is what builds a brand's reputation.

When Nendo designed stores for the Spanish shoe brand Camper, Sato knew Camper shoes neither help you run faster nor say anything about your status. So he set out to help people discover the pleasure of walking, and showed it with pairs of shoes strolling freely through the store. The shoes drifting through the air were not beauty or whimsy for its own sake. Sato took them from the comfort of the shoes themselves: a kind of magic that "makes you fall in love with walking."

![Camper, Paris](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150538NLmswIVDryY1BfoZ.jpg-w600)

![Camper, Shinjuku](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150539lH3JWUEQApIBuzfo.jpg-w600)

![Camper, San Francisco](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150539d2zGLSHIXAkYRFv0.jpg-w600)

This is how Nendo became an international studio. Selling the product well matters, but raising the value of the company's and the product's brand matters more than short-term profit.

Its list of big-name clients is long: Coca-Cola, Hermès, Nissin, Lotte, Puma, Issey Miyake, Tod's, Shu Uemura, Toshiba, Häagen-Dazs, Camper, Starbucks, Isetan, Elecom, Swarovski, NEC and more.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150539x1sOlWcmzjo5SkVC.jpg-w600)

![Window displays for Hermès in Tokyo and Yokohama, 2012](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150543J5ThrYuSpE7BGbj3.jpg-w600)

![Packaging for Shu Uemura, 2014](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150544YGU5LoWcCqa6ejx2.jpg-w600)

![A Christmas ice cream cake for Häagen-Dazs, 2014](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150544bVF9hIPKnBkNgL2m.jpg-w600)

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150545bkpEwqj4Xz6KdutI.jpg-w600)

![A briefcase for Tod's](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031505466CXpVOtGzslYfFW5.jpg-w600)

Still, marketing flourishes are useless without solid design underneath.

To Sato, design and marketing cannot be separated. "Suppose one studio turns 100-point ideas into 40-point designs, and another reliably turns 70-point ideas into 100-point designs. It's obvious which one a client will choose." That is how he understands creative work.

This is not only a question of ideas. It is also a question of how Sato runs his studio: how he builds the conditions in which ideas can actually be carried out.

The first step is understanding what the client expects. A few questions and answers won't do it. You may need to know the company's history, its current situation and future direction, its short-term goals, its product positioning, its competitors, and its past successes and failures. Sato calls this the "project warm-up," and he considers it even more important than the proposal itself.

If, after talking with a client, he still can't grasp what they want, he turns the job down.

Many ideas are found during the warm-up. Straining for one 100-point idea is hard. What Sato goes after instead is "lots of 70-point ideas. If you can shape ideas three times faster than usual, you can present three times as many proposals in the same schedule and spend the remaining two-thirds of the time refining them. That way, even if the first proposal fails, there's plenty of time to recover, and the client trusts you more."

Sato admits that no other studio puts as much weight on speed.

Last April we reported that [Nendo was running nearly 400 projects at once](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/9020.html). Sato compares himself to a fish that might die if it stopped swimming. "Sometimes I feel I can't keep up with myself. I'm thinking about so many things, and I have so many ideas I need to get out. It's like breathing or eating."

Doesn't he ever run out of ideas? His answer: "Always stay curious about everything in the world." That sounds like a greeting-card slogan, but his ideas come at any moment because of how intensely he concentrates. He never does anything special to provoke inspiration, and as a result he values what he notices in ordinary life and work all the more.

What is the point of a staircase when no one is climbing it, a lamp during the day or while you sleep, a television when no one is watching? Most people never think about this. Sato wants to make use of the "rest time" of everyday objects. For the interior of the ILLOIHA OMOTESANDO gym, he brought a climbing wall, normally an outdoor feature, inside, making it the centerpiece of the space, so that it looks good even when no one is climbing.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031505460pk2yB7qJNAshoLK.jpg-w600)

![The climbing wall at the ILLOIHA OMOTESANDO gym](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150547RHUF6YXgQkLqGMET.jpg-w600)

"I don't do anything except think about design projects." Even on business trips abroad, he tries to go no farther than his hotel, restaurants and meeting rooms. You might conclude that a man who talks like this must be dull. Then how do you explain the wit in his work that makes people smile? Remember that the studio's guiding aim is "giving people a small '!' moment."

He has distilled his thinking into ten methods, among them creating a sense of "something out of place," breaking "balance," and designing by "taking a step back." All of them are ways to produce that "!" moment.

At the core of the Nendo way of thinking is a phrase Sato repeats often: "The more ordinary, the more wondrous."

It resembles Kenya Hara's idea of "looking at the familiar as if for the first time." But Hara cares about the process of redesigning ordinary objects through ideas and craft. Sato has always believed that "what is truly rich and profound is always the 'extraordinary' scattered through everyday life." He starts with a cup and widens his view step by step: what kind of table it belongs on, what style it calls for, who will use it, what surrounds it.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150547h1yzJDUHI0BZRYru.jpg-w600)

![Cups for Starbucks Japan, with three different patterns on the bottom for Americano, latte and caramel macchiato](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150548Rdpvb6EuhJslFCmi.jpg-w600)

Meji, an umbrella stand Nendo released this January, takes its form from the gaps between floor tiles. It uses grooves instead of holes, so it doesn't spoil the look of a room when no umbrellas are in it.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150548aIHj7UrnoKTqmWXE.jpg-w600)

![The Meji umbrella stand](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150549L7qEFvJulTW6YcVd.jpg-w600)

Then there is the mobile cushion, made for the way young people live with their devices. The market is full of stands for phones and tablets, but none is as comfortable as a cushion. On the patchwork-fabric cushions, Nendo left openings along the outer seams, so you can prop up a screen while lounging on a sofa or in bed.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150549MqLPkpIKr0xduo1U.jpg-w600)

![The mobile cushion](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150550nVRrhw5YqgcIFmTi.jpg-w600)

The Kame suitcase has a lid of soft woven material that folds back section by section, so you can open it in tight spaces. Both sides open too, so you no longer have to lay the case flat every time you want something out or in.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150550lKC5WUzXF6dGhvjg.jpg-w600)

![The Kame suitcase](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150551w0JlrmZE4hvbaW7L.jpg-w600)

Nendo's designs all start from ordinary things within reach. They just think one step further than the rest of us.

Take mixing things that don't belong together. Chocolate pencils are a fine example: chocolate in different cocoa strengths shaped like pencils, sold with a sharpener of their own. The shavings are no longer waste but a garnish for food, and that is the fun of the design.

![Chocolate pencils](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150551sKJhOtDoLRSpqwf7.jpg-w600)

Then there is the game between curiosity and concealment. Everyone is curious, so hiding part of an object draws people in. On a ruler for Nendo's own brand, by | n, the white markings vanish against a light background and the black markings vanish against a dark one. The [Border Table](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/16078.html) we featured earlier is another example of concealment at work.

![Contrast Ruler](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150552pHQ5lUkzOK97FjuT.jpg-w600)

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150552G0iD5cReLUzY2boP.jpg-w600)

![Border Table](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/2016070315055248IzJ36tleTcZQrh.jpg-w600)

QDaily's design section has covered many Nendo products and exhibitions. Try to pin down a signature style and one thing stands out: Nendo takes strict, measured minimalism and softens it with a childlike humor, which makes the work look more like a product of Japanese pop culture.

Look through Nendo's catalogue and you will find plenty of small delights that are both useful and good-looking: Stay-brella, an umbrella that stands up on its own without leaning on anything; Bubbles, a home fragrance that pictures scent drifting through a room as soap bubbles; a nine-cube bookshelf that stretches; and slippers that stack away like wizards' hats.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150553Tsh3ZVzNt2bXyEFO.jpg-w600)

![Stay-brella](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150554HTLksewEQxGV1h3n.jpg-w600)

![Bubbles home fragrance](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150554mhejpoZcAHRJwX4I.jpg-w600)

![The stretchable bookshelf](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150554G6zo3vmKlYha1EBT.gif-w600Gif)

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703150555MEefRqAQnrNPKSLz.jpg-w600)

![Slippers that stack away like wizards' hats](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031505560B4pJawGgmSTCn5F.jpg-w600)

Japanese industrial design often expresses itself through a traditional Eastern way of thinking and feeling. Nendo's success comes from Western and Japanese design thinking working together. On one side, it runs design as a business, meeting clients' needs quickly and precisely. On the other, it keeps the Japanese command of detail.

Many designers can learn from this approach. And even if you don't design anything, whenever you face the problem of how to get an idea out of your head and into the world, Sato's way of looking is worth borrowing.
